I was on the go the whole time without any breaks during that period.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if the current 'heavy, flat' low phase has lasted continuously for at least two weeks without any significant improvement in your mood or interest in activities?\n\nPatient: Yes, it has lasted much longer than just two weeks. This heavy, flat feeling has been going on steadily for about five months now without any break or improvement. It just feels like one long, exhausting stretch that I can't seem to shake.\n\nDoctor: To confirm, the most recent 'revved up' episode lasted less than 4 weeks, and the current 'heavy, flat' episode has lasted more than 2 weeks, correct?\n\nPatient: Yes, that is exactly correct. The revved-up period lasted for just about two to three weeks during the peak of tax season, while this heavy, flat feeling has been dragging on steadily for about five months now, which is much longer than two weeks.\n\nDoctor: To further clarify, you're saying the most recent 'revved up' episode lasted less than 4 weeks, but can you specify if it met the full criteria for a manic episode, such as lasting at least 7 consecutive days, or if it was shorter?\n\nPatient: Yes, it definitely lasted for about two to three weeks straight, which is well over seven consecutive days. During those weeks, I felt consistently energized, buzzed, and barely slept every single day, rather than it just being a few short days.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience any psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations or delusions, during either the 'revved up' or 'heavy, flat' episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced anything like that at all. I've never had any hallucinations, delusions, or anything of that nature during either my high or low periods.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned the 'revved up' period lasted for about two to three weeks, but can you confirm if, during that time, you experienced any significant impairment in social or occupational functioning, or if you required hospitalization due to the severity of your symptoms?\n\nPatient: No, I didn't need to be hospitalized, and I actually felt highly productive and on top of the world rather than impaired. While my coworkers noticed I was talking fast and a bit snappy, I was getting a ton of work done; the actual mistakes and social withdrawal only started once I crashed into this low state.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether, during your 'revved up' periods, you experienced at least three or more symptoms such as inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, more talkative than usual, flight of ideas, distractibility, increase in goal-directed activity, or excessive involvement in pleasurable activities that could lead to painful consequences?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely experienced several of those. I only needed three to four hours of sleep a night without feeling tired, and my coworkers joked that I was talking a mile a minute because my thoughts were racing with so many ideas. I also had this huge wave of confidence where I took on way too many tasks at once, fully believing I could easily start my own bookkeeping firm.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the symptoms during your 'revved up' period caused significant distress or impairment in your social or occupational functioning, or if they were more of a subjective experience without major consequences?\n\nPatient: During that revved-up time, I didn't feel distressed or impaired at all—I actually felt on top of the world, extremely productive, and full of energy despite barely sleeping. While I was a bit snappy with coworkers and talked really fast, it didn't cause any major problems or consequences at the time. I didn't experience those high feelings mixed with depressive symptoms at the same time, though; it was a very distinct switch where I was either highly revved up or crashed into this heavy low.\n\nDoctor: Did the symptoms during your 'revved up' period meet the full criteria for a manic episode, which includes lasting at least 7 consecutive days and causing significant impairment, or did they more closely align with hypomanic episode criteria, which involves less severe symptoms and less impairment?\n\nPatient: It definitely aligns more with the hypomanic description because I didn't feel impaired at all during those revved-up weeks. I felt incredibly productive, energetic, and on top of the world, even though I was barely sleeping and talking a mile a minute. The actual impairment, mistakes at work, and struggle to function only started after I crashed into my current low state.\n\nDoctor: Given that your 'revved up' periods have been less severe and didn't cause significant impairment, but have switched to long 'heavy, flat' lows, do you think the pattern of your episodes, with the recent low phase lasting about five months, suggests a more chronic condition, or do you feel like you're experiencing distinct episodes of highs and lows?"
